analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover at least 48 hours of hospital stay for mothers and newborns after birth.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill guaranteeing new mothers at least 48 hours of covered hospital care won approval from the Senate labor committee with 52 cosponsors, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any health plan that covers childbirth to pay for a minimum of 48 hours of inpatient care after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean section, without insurers requiring advance permission for the longer stay. If a mother and her doctor agree to leave earlier, the plan must cover a follow-up visit by a qualified nurse or provider within 72 hours, including the option of a home visit. It also bars plans from paying mothers to opt for shorter stays or penalizing providers who follow the rules, and lets states keep or adopt stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Women giving birth and their newborns who are covered by employer or individual health plans. They gain a guaranteed minimum hospital stay after delivery, protection against insurers pushing early discharge with cash rebates, and coverage for a timely follow-up visit if they do leave early.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Mothers and newborns on health plans

how_it_helps.text: Health plans that cover childbirth must pay for at least 48 hours of inpatient care after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean, without the provider needing advance authorization from the plan.

If the mother's provider, consulting with her, decides on an earlier discharge, the plan must cover timely post-delivery follow-up care within 72 hours, delivered by a registered nurse, physician, nurse practitioner, nurse midwife, or physician assistant, with the mother having the option of care in her home.

Plans may not offer mothers monetary payments or rebates to request less than the required stay, and may not penalize or reduce the reimbursement of providers who treat patients consistent with the law.
Each plan must send enrollees and policyholders prominent written notice of these coverage rights within 120 days of enactment and annually afterward.

The rules are enforced by state insurance commissioners for health plans and under ERISA for employee benefit plans, and the bill does not override state laws that give patients even stronger protections, such as leaving the length of stay entirely to the attending provider.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and group purchasers that fund health benefits, through the added cost of longer covered stays and follow-up visits, which are typically passed into premiums shared by employers and enrollees.

drawbacks.text: The committee substitute softened the original bill: instead of an unconditional 48-hour guarantee, a plan can cover an earlier discharge if the provider agrees in consultation with the mother and the plan pays for follow-up care, so the full stay is no longer automatic.

The bill itself orders federal studies and an advisory panel on the appropriate length of hospital stays and on the financial incentives affecting mothers' and newborns' health, an acknowledgment that Congress was mandating coverage without settled evidence on the best length of stay.

The definitions exclude several kinds of arrangements, including fixed indemnity, short-term limited duration, supplemental, and dental- or vision-only coverage, so those policies would not have to meet the minimum-stay standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the mothers and newborns affected, the benefit is concrete and timely: it ends the practice of insurers pushing families out of the hospital within hours of birth, and it guarantees professional follow-up for those who leave early. The cost is a modest per-birth increase in covered services spread across all plan enrollees, and the main design weakness is the substitute's early-discharge option, which trades a guaranteed stay for a promise of follow-up care that depends on families actually receiving it.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate labor committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in July 1996, but no senator ever got to vote on it before that Congress ended, and the House never considered it.

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. Bill Bradley on June 27, 1995, the bill was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which held hearings that September.

On April 17, 1996, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was formally reported to the Senate on July 19, 1996, with a written report and additional views.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 505 on July 19, 1996, which meant it was ready for the Senate to take up, but no floor vote ever occurred in the remaining months of the 104th Congress.
The bill drew 52 cosponsors split 20 Republicans and 32 Democrats, and the committee's Republican chair reported it, yet it never reached the floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

The same minimum-stay requirement did become federal law later in 1996, when Congress attached it to an unrelated spending bill enacted that September, so mothers and newborns received the protection despite this bill itself dying without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because S. 969 never came to a vote, health plans avoided the 48-hour mandate for the remainder of the 104th Congress. In practical terms mothers lost little in the end: Congress enacted the identical minimum-stay guarantee into law that same year through an appropriations bill, so newborn families got the benefit while the insurers' delay was the only thing the stall achieved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers got a delay; mothers got the law anyway

for.name: Sen. Bill Bradley
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 41 original cosponsors and made introductory remarks in 1995 and again after the committee reported it in 1996.

for.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Held committee hearings on the bill, ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and formally reported it to the Senate in July 1996.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor time for the bill after it was placed on the Senate calendar in July 1996, and no Senate vote occurred before the Congress ended.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.role: Insurers and managed care plans opposing mandated minimum maternity stays
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed laws requiring minimum hospital stays after childbirth, which reversed the industry's cost-saving practice of early discharge, popularly known as drive-through deliveries.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: 52 senators cosponsored the bill, split 20 Republicans and 32 Democrats, and the committee's Republican chair reported it favorably, so its failure came from a missing floor vote rather than a party-line split.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill forces plans that cover childbirth to pay for minimum 48- and 96-hour stays plus follow-up care, directly reversing the cost savings of early discharge. The industry's interest in shorter stays runs against what mothers and newborns need.

industries.industry: Employers and other group purchasers funding health benefits
industries.note: Employers whose plans must meet the standards would bear somewhat higher benefit costs, though their employees and dependents receive the protection in return.
Longer covered stays and guaranteed follow-up visits by nurses, midwives, and physicians mean more reimbursed care, and the bill bars plans from penalizing providers who follow it.
